outcome: No accepted resolution, disproof or partial result on Brocard's conjecture has appeared since 26 January 2024. Three in-window items bear on it: an unrefereed arXiv preprint (Grah, Dec 2024) whose Proposition 6.11 gives Brocard's inequality if its Theorem 6.8 (two primes between successive squares) holds, which I could not verify; an unrefereed Preprints.org claim (Vega, Aug-Sep 2024) that an Oppermann-conjecture proof also settles Brocard; and a finite computer check to n = 4x10^5 (MathWorld, Jan 2025), which does not settle a universal claim.
problem_asks: Part 1: for every n >= 2, with p_n the nth prime, the open interval between p_n^2 and p_{n+1}^2 contains at least four primes; equivalently pi(p_{n+1}^2) - pi(p_n^2) >= 4. This quantifies over all n, so it is an infinite claim. Part 2: the bound asked is four, not two or three. Part 3: the exception. The bullet excludes '2^2 and 3^2'. Read in the n >= 2 form, this removes only the interval (2^2, 3^2) = (4, 9), which holds two primes (5 and 7), and keeps (3^2, 5^2) = (9, 25), which holds five primes. Read literally as excluding every interval with an endpoint 2^2 or 3^2, (9, 25) is also excluded. The bullet's wording does not settle which reading is meant. Part 4: the intervals are between squares of consecutive primes, not between consecutive integer squares (that is Legendre's conjecture).

events.what_happened: G. Spencer-Brown, Laws of Form (London: Allen & Unwin, 1969), Appendix 8 (number theory). Per the 2025 commentary abstract, the appendix gives proofs that there are at least two primes between any consecutive squared numbers, and the commentary says the existence of primes between squares has been a conjecture since Legendre. This is a book, not a journal article. I did not read the appendix itself; the description comes from the commentary abstract (see Flagg, Kauffman and Sahoo, 2025, below).
events.revisions: First edition 1969 (Allen & Unwin, per the Wikipedia Laws of Form article). Later editions not checked.
events.delivers: Claimed: at least two primes between every pair of consecutive squares. This is the same statement that Grah's Theorem 6.8 claims. The commentary does not say Spencer-Brown stated Brocard's conjecture. Inference (mine, not the source's): by the counting step in Grah's Proposition 6.11, a two-prime statement for all consecutive squares would also give Brocard's inequality for n >= 2.
events.remains: If the claim fails, everything in problem_asks. If it holds, Part 1 follows by the counting step described above (my inference, not stated by the source).

checked_by.who: J. M. Flagg, Louis H. Kauffman and Divyamaan Sahoo
checked_by.qualification: Authors of a 61-page arXiv commentary guiding readers through the appendix. Credentials not checked.
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a commentary explaining the appendix. Said its proofs mix rigorous arguments with stated facts that 'would be considered conjectures by most number theorists'. Did not state whether the proofs are complete and did not name the conjectural lemmas.

events.doubts: The 2025 commentary says the proofs depend on stated facts that most number theorists would count as conjectures, and it does not say which. I found no journal refereeing. Chamberland and Straub (arXiv 2602.22502, Feb 2026) state that no unconditional result of at least two primes between consecutive squares is known and treat Legendre's conjecture as open; their review does not mention Spencer-Brown's appendix (I did not check its reference list in full).
events.direction: Toward proof of the two-prime statement (claimed). Brocard follows only through a counting step, and the source does not say Brocard is claimed.

events.what_happened: Adway Mitra, Goutam Paul and Ushnish Sarkar, 'Some Conjectures on the Number of Primes in Certain Intervals', arXiv:0906.0104 (math.NT). They propose sharper versions of Legendre's conjecture and state: 'we show that Brocard's Conjecture can be proved assuming our improved version of Legendre's Conjecture.'
events.revisions: v1 only (30 May 2009).
events.delivers: Conditional implication only: Brocard's inequality follows from the authors' improved Legendre-type conjecture. Restriction: the improved conjecture is itself unproven.
events.remains: Unconditional Brocard (all of problem_asks). The improved Legendre-type conjecture is also open.
events.direction: Conditional implication. Does not prove or refute Brocard unconditionally.

events.what_happened: Asia Furones, 'A Single Proof to Four Conjectures', arXiv:1205.6365 (math.GM). The v5 abstract (24 Sep 2012) claims that for every natural number n >= 2 there is at least one prime between n and n + ceil(sqrt(n)), and that this 'demonstrates the Oppermann and Brocard conjectures, therefore, the Legendre and Andrica conjectures.' The abs page for the paper shows only an arXiv administrative note saying it was withdrawn because of the use of a pseudonym, in violation of arXiv policy. v7 (19 Nov 2012) is marked withdrawn. I did not read v1 to v4 or v6, so I cannot say which version first carried the Brocard claim.
events.revisions: v1 29 May 2012; v2 4 Jun 2012; v3 1 Aug 2012; v4 18 Sep 2012; v5 24 Sep 2012; v6 9 Oct 2012; v7 19 Nov 2012 (withdrawn).
events.delivers: Claimed (v5 abstract): Brocard's conjecture, via a statement about a prime in each short interval (n, n + ceil(sqrt(n))) for n >= 2. I did not check whether the stated interval result implies Brocard's inequality.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, if the claim fails. The later versions are withdrawn, and the content I could read is only the v5 abstract.
events.doubts: The abs page gives an arXiv administrative note about pseudonymous authorship, and the later versions are withdrawn. The sources disagree on who withdrew the later version: the abs page gives the admin note, while the v5 page says the author withdrew 'a newer version'. The step from the interval statement to Oppermann and Brocard is not shown in the abstract.

withdrawn.what: v7 (submitted 19 Nov 2012) marked withdrawn. The abs page shows an arXiv administrative note citing pseudonym use.
withdrawn.by: unclear: arXiv admin note on the abs page; the v5 page says the author withdrew the newer version

events.direction: Toward proof (claimed in v5). Withdrawn at v7.

events.what_happened: Germán Paz, 'On Legendre's, Brocard's, Andrica's, and Oppermann's Conjectures', arXiv:1310.1323. Reports that every block of n consecutive integers strictly between n^2 and (n+1)^2 contains a prime, for every n <= 1,193,806,023 (computation). Shows that a positive answer for all n would imply Legendre's, Brocard's, Andrica's and Oppermann's conjectures. Presented as a conditional implication, not a proof of Brocard.
events.revisions: v1 19 Sep 2013; v2 2 Apr 2014 (title and abstract modified, references added at a reviewer's suggestion).
events.delivers: Conditional: if the block-prime statement holds for all n, Brocard follows. Unconditionally, a finite check of the block statement for n <= 1,193,806,023, which is an instance count and not a check of Brocard's own statement.
events.remains: Unconditional Brocard (all of problem_asks), and the block statement beyond the checked range.
events.direction: Conditional implication. Neither proves nor refutes Brocard.

events.what_happened: Apoloniusz Tyszka, 'A common approach to three open problems in number theory', arXiv:1506.08655, published in Discrete Mathematics Letters 12 (2023), 66-72. Its Hypothesis 2 concerns x!+1 = y^2, which is Brocard's problem (the namesake factorial equation), not Brocard's conjecture on primes. The other hypotheses concern composite Fermat-type numbers and x(x+1) = y!. The paper describes semi-algorithms that never terminate.
events.revisions: v1 24 Jun 2015; v61 10 May 2023 (last revision shown); published Discrete Mathematics Letters 12 (2023).
events.delivers: Hypothesis-based statements on the namesake equation x!+1 = y^2. Nothing on primes between consecutive prime squares.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.

checked_by.who: Discrete Mathematics Letters (journal listed in the arXiv abstract page)
checked_by.qualification: journal of record listed for the paper
checked_by.what_they_did: published (per the arXiv journal reference); refereeing not checked

events.doubts: Namesake only; not a result on this statement.
events.direction: Not bearing on this statement (namesake problem: Brocard's problem).

events.what_happened: Ahmad Sabihi, 'On solutions of some of unsolved problems in number theory, specifically on the distribution of primes', arXiv:1605.01722. The abstract claims to 'solve some famous conjectures on the distribution of primes', listing Legendre's, Andrica's, Oppermann's, Brocard's, Cramér's and Shanks' conjectures and five Smarandache conjectures. The method uses Firoozbakht's conjecture (which the author says he proved) and Kourbatov's theorem. Per search excerpts of the body (not read in full by me), Brocard follows from Oppermann's conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 5 May 2016; v2 9 May 2016; v3 5 Jun 2016; v4 1 Jan 2018; v5 15 Jan 2018 (current).
events.delivers: Claimed (abstract): a solution of Brocard's conjecture. Per the excerpts, the route is through Oppermann's conjecture, which is open, so the claim is conditional on that. The Firoozbakht input is itself claimed by the author.
events.remains: Unconditional Brocard, if the Oppermann route is the only one. Also the other ten listed conjectures.
events.doubts: One short arXiv paper claims to settle eleven named problems (six named conjectures plus five Smarandache conjectures). Its method depends on Firoozbakht's conjecture, which the abstract says the author proved himself and which I did not check. The Brocard step, per excerpts, rests on Oppermann's conjecture, which is open. No peer-reviewed publication or expert engagement found.
events.direction: Toward proof (claimed). Route per excerpts is conditional on Oppermann's conjecture.

events.what_happened: Matt Visser, 'Strong version of Andrica's conjecture', arXiv:1812.02762. The abstract states that the strong and standard Brocard conjectures 'are unconditionally and explicitly verified for all primes p < 2^32 (approx. 4.294 x 10^9)'. It presents this as a consequence of an implication chain (strong Andrica implies Oppermann, which implies the strong and standard Brocard conjectures), and says the strong Andrica form is verified for all primes below 2^64. The abstract does not describe the computation. Journal reference: International Mathematical Forum 14(4) (2019), 181-188.
events.revisions: v1 6 Dec 2018; v2 19 Feb 2019; v3 9 May 2019 (current).
events.delivers: A finite verification: Brocard's inequality for every prime p < 2^32, which is roughly n up to 2x10^8. Brocard is universal, so this finite range does not settle it. The implication chain is the author's and I did not check it.
events.remains: All primes p >= 2^32, which is the whole universal claim.

checked_by.who: International Mathematical Forum (journal reference on the arXiv abstract page)
checked_by.qualification: journal of record listed for the paper
checked_by.what_they_did: published (per the arXiv journal reference); no referee report or independent verification found

events.doubts: The computation is asserted, not described: the abstract gives the range but not the method, and the chain runs through Oppermann's conjecture. The range (p < 2^32, roughly n up to 2x10^8) is far larger than the n <= 4x10^5 that MathWorld states in January 2025. I did not resolve which is right, or whether the two use different verification.
events.direction: Verifies finitely many instances (consistent with the conjecture). No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Sundarakannan Mahilmaran, 'Existence of primes between two consecutive squares', arXiv:1908.08995 (16 Aug 2019). Claims to 'prove the conjecture holds true' for Legendre's conjecture (a prime between consecutive integer squares). Does not mention Brocard's conjecture. A Pith Review page (not opened; seen in a search excerpt) reports an automated referee objection that the key step assumes the prime it should derive.
events.revisions: v1 only (16 Aug 2019).
events.delivers: Claimed proof of Legendre's conjecture (neighbour, not Brocard). Per Wikipedia, Legendre's conjecture gives only a weak Brocard statement (two primes), so even an accepted proof would not deliver Part 1.
events.remains: Brocard's conjecture entirely (not touched). Legendre itself, if the proof fails.

checked_by.qualification: AI referee site; not a human reading
checked_by.what_they_did: Reported (per a search excerpt; the page was not opened) that the argument reduces to a prime that it assumes rather than derives

events.doubts: Single-version abstract claim of an open conjecture. The only objection I found is an automated referee review, read second-hand.
events.direction: Toward proof of Legendre's conjecture (claimed). Not Brocard.

events.what_happened: Jan Feliksiak, 'The Brocard conjecture', ScienceOpen Preprints (not on arXiv). Per a search excerpt of its abstract, the author 'implements a least lower bound to prove the conjecture', and develops upper and lower bounds on the number of primes in the interval, using twin primes as the shortest such interval. The ScienceOpen pages returned HTTP 403, so I did not read the text. Sources disagree on the year: 2020 in one search summary, 2021 in another, and one excerpt gives 'February 2021'.
events.revisions: None found. Not read.
events.delivers: Claimed (per excerpt): a proof of Brocard's conjecture by a lower bound on primes in the interval. I could not read the argument, so I cannot state which parts of problem_asks it covers.
events.remains: Unknown; not read.
events.doubts: Its page, per an excerpt, says it is not peer-reviewed and is open for review on ScienceOpen. I found no acceptance or critique. The argument was not read.
events.direction: Toward proof (claimed). Not read.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'Note for the Prime Gaps', EasyChair Preprint 13133 (posted 29 Apr 2024; the page lists six versions). Claims to prove Andrica's conjecture (the difference of square roots of consecutive primes is below 1), using the divergence of the sum of reciprocals of primes, per the abstract as I read it. Does not mention Brocard's conjecture. Same author as the Oppermann note below.
events.revisions: Six versions listed on the page. A search excerpt reports that v6 (12 May 2024) assumes an inequality holds for all n above 1.3x10^16 instead. Versions not checked one by one.
events.delivers: Claimed proof of Andrica's conjecture (neighbour). Not a Brocard result.
events.remains: Brocard's conjecture entirely (not touched).
events.doubts: The page says 'There isn't a verified solution to Andrica's conjecture yet' while also saying 'we prove' it. Later versions are reported as conditional (see revisions). Preprint; no review found.
events.direction: Toward proof of Andrica's conjecture (claimed). No bearing on Brocard.

events.what_happened: Mohamed Imteaz Karimullah, 'Solution of Brocard's Problem', Indian Journal of Advanced Mathematics 4(1), 25-28 (2024), DOI 10.54105/ijam.B1174.04010424. Claims that there are no solutions of n! + 1 = m^2 beyond (4,5), (5,11) and (7,71). This is Brocard's problem (the namesake factorial equation), not Brocard's conjecture on primes.
events.revisions: Zenodo record created 25 Jul 2024; Zenodo publication 30 Jul 2024. Journal publication date 30 Apr 2024 as listed on the Zenodo page.
events.delivers: Claimed finiteness result for the namesake equation n! + 1 = m^2. Nothing on primes between consecutive prime squares.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (different question).
events.doubts: Namesake only. Abstract read; no review seen. The Erdos #398 thread lists the equation as open, so the claim, if right, would settle that question.
events.direction: Claims the namesake equation has no further solutions. Not bearing on this statement.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'A Note on Oppermann's Conjecture', Preprints.org manuscript 202408.1161 (not peer-reviewed, per the site). Four versions, reported as posted 16 Aug to 12 Sep 2024. Claims a proof of Oppermann's conjecture and says the same argument 'simultaneously establishes Andrica's, Legendre's, and Brocard's conjectures' (a sentence quoted in a search excerpt of v1). The preprints.org pages returned HTTP 403, so I did not read the version texts. Excerpts disagree on the method: one has v1 and v2 on Euler-Maclaurin and harmonic numbers, and v4 on the square-root function on prime inequalities. v3 is reported as conditional on an inequality for primes above 10^8.
events.revisions: Four versions, 16 Aug to 12 Sep 2024 (per excerpt). v3 reported as conditional on a Chebyshev-function inequality for primes above 10^8. v4 reported to use the square-root function; excerpts conflict on whether v4 still claims Brocard outright (one says the Brocard claim is unchanged; another says v4 frames Brocard as following if Oppermann's conjecture holds).
events.delivers: Claimed, not verified by me: Oppermann's conjecture for all n, and Brocard's conjecture as a consequence (the note treats Brocard as a corollary of its Oppermann proof). Whether the Brocard claim is unconditional depends on the version, which I could not read. Restriction: the version reported as conditional rests on an inequality for primes above 10^8.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks if the Oppermann argument fails. No version has been accepted, and no public refutation was found.
events.doubts: Self-posted preprint, labelled not peer-reviewed by Preprints.org. The method changed between versions (Euler-Maclaurin to square-root). The version reported as conditional rests on an inequality for primes above 10^8 whose proof I did not find. The same author's Andrica note (above) has a similar pattern of claiming a proof while saying no verified solution exists, and its later version is reported as conditional on an inequality for all n above 1.3x10^16. The Brocard claim is a corollary of the Oppermann claim, so it stands or falls with it. No outside engagement found in searches.
events.direction: Toward proof (claimed, through Oppermann's conjecture). Not accepted, and the version texts were not read by me.

events.what_happened: Jacques Grah, 'Conditional Bounds for Prime Gaps with Applications', arXiv:2412.12311 (math.NT), posted 16 Dec 2024. The title and Section 2 frame the paper as conditional on Conjecture 1.1 (d_n < sqrt(2) p_{n+1}^(1/2), with d_n = p_{n+1} - p_n). Section 2's one-prime result (Theorem 2.3, 'There is a prime between two successive perfect squares') is proved only conditionally on Conjecture 1.1. Section 6.2, headed 'Oppermann's and Brocard's Conjectures', contains Theorem 6.8, stated with no hypothesis: 'There are at least two prime numbers between successive perfect squares.' Its proof, as I read it, is by contradiction and cites Theorem 6.6 (a statement about the fractional parts mu_n of sqrt(p_n): mu_n is bounded below by 1/2 at the same time as mu_{n+1} < 1/2). I could not find a proof of Theorem 6.6 in the text I could read. Proposition 6.11 then states pi(p_{n+1}^2) - pi(p_n^2) >= 2 d_n for n >= 1, with a one-line proof that at least two primes lie between each pair of consecutive squares from p_n^2 to (p_n + d_n)^2. The paper calls Proposition 6.11 'a subsequent result which refines Brocard's conjecture'. It does not state the conclusion >= 4.
events.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2024; v2 29 Aug 2025 (current). Theorem 6.8 and Proposition 6.11 appear in v1 as well (checked in the v1 HTML, Section 6.2). The title and Section 2 framing are the same in both versions.
events.delivers: Claimed, as the text presents it: an unconditional statement that every pair of successive perfect squares has at least two primes between them (Theorem 6.8), and Proposition 6.11, which gives pi(p_{n+1}^2) - pi(p_n^2) >= 2 d_n for n >= 1. My inference, not the paper's: for n >= 2 the primes are odd, so d_n >= 2, and Proposition 6.11 then gives pi(p_{n+1}^2) - pi(p_n^2) >= 4, which is Part 1 of problem_asks. If Theorem 6.8 and the proof of Theorem 6.6 hold, this preprint delivers all of Part 1 (and by the same route, the Legendre one-prime statement, which the paper otherwise derives only conditionally). Restriction: the Brocard form depends entirely on Theorem 6.8, and Theorem 6.8 depends on Theorem 6.6, which I could not read.
events.remains: If Theorem 6.6 or 6.8 fails: all of problem_asks. Proposition 6.11 is a counting step; it has no independent open part. The paper itself does not draw the >= 4 conclusion, so the judging pass should read Part 1 as the author's implied claim, not a theorem the author states.
events.doubts: (1) Internal tension. Theorem 6.8 (two primes between successive squares, no hypothesis) would imply Legendre's conjecture (at least one prime). The Introduction describes Legendre's conjecture as 'still waiting for an answer', and Section 2 derives the one-prime statement only conditionally on Conjecture 1.1. A paper that proves the stronger statement unconditionally while deriving the weaker one conditionally is inconsistent unless the parts are independent in a way I did not see. (2) Theorem 6.6, on which Theorem 6.8's proof depends, has no proof in the text I read: the HTML copy I could reach is truncated at Lemma 9.7 and the PDF returned only compressed streams. (3) Section 6.1 uses Legendre's conjecture for the bound d_n <= 2 floor(p_n) ('because of Legendre's conjecture') in the context of consecutive squares. I could not establish whether Theorem 6.6 or 6.8 inherits that dependence. (4) The same two-prime statement was claimed in 1969 by Spencer-Brown (above). The 2025 commentary says those proofs rest partly on facts most number theorists would count as conjectures. (5) Later review does not cite it: Chamberland and Straub (arXiv 2602.22502, Feb 2026) treat Legendre's conjecture as open and state no unconditional two-prime result. No citing paper found. (6) The abstract, as I could read it, does not mention Brocard, Legendre or Oppermann. It states a proof of pi((n+1)^k) - pi(n^k) >= pi(2^k) (k >= 2, n >= 1) and presents its main inequality as a posit.
events.direction: Toward proof: if Theorem 6.8 and Proposition 6.11 hold, Brocard's inequality (at least four primes for every n >= 2) follows. The paper presents Proposition 6.11 as a refinement of Brocard's conjecture and does not state the conclusion.

events.what_happened: MathWorld entry 'Brocard's Conjecture' (updated 12 Jan 2025, credited to E. W. Weisstein): 'The conjecture is true for 2<=n<=4x10^5 (E. Weisstein, Jan. 12, 2025) but remains unproven.' OEIS A050216 (number of primes between consecutive prime squares) has a comment that a(n) >= 4 holds up to at least n = 4x10^5 (Eric W. Weisstein), with Mathematica code credited to Weisstein (10 Jan 2025) and Maple code to R. J. Mathar (27 Jan 2025). Neither page names a method beyond the code credits.
events.revisions: MathWorld page updated 12 Jan 2025 per its status line; OEIS page carries a 'Last modified' footer that refers to the site, not this sequence.
events.delivers: A finite computer check of the statement for n up to 4x10^5. Finite instances of a universal claim; no counterexample and no change to any counted quantity beyond the instances checked.
events.remains: All n > 4x10^5, which is the whole universal claim.

checked_by.qualification: MathWorld editor; the computation's code is credited to him on OEIS A050216
checked_by.what_they_did: Computed the check (Mathematica code credited on OEIS A050216)

machine_checked.system: Mathematica (code credited to E. W. Weisstein on OEIS A050216)

events.directly_checkable: The sequence A050216 is computable directly from prime counts at consecutive prime squares; the check at n <= 4x10^5 is reproducible from the OEIS b-file, which I did not download.
events.doubts: The MathWorld and OEIS pages give the range but not the method. The range is much smaller than the p < 2^32 range that Visser (2018) claims, and the two sources disagree on the largest checked range. I did not resolve this.
events.direction: Finite instances consistent with the conjecture. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: Adrian W. Dudek and Daniel R. Johnston, 'Almost primes between all squares', arXiv:2501.18048. Proves that for all n >= 1 there is a number between n^2 and (n+1)^2 with at most four prime factors, using a computation of Sorenson and Webster and an explicit linear sieve. Not about primes, and not about prime squares.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jan 2025; v2 15 Feb 2025; v3 24 Jun 2025 (current).
events.delivers: Almost-prime result for consecutive integer squares. Neighbour: different intervals (n^2 to (n+1)^2) and almost primes, not primes between consecutive prime squares.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Not bearing on this statement.

events.what_happened: Ken Clements, Substack post 'Beyond Binary Claims: Mathematical Discovery Through Human-AI Collaboration Part 6', dated 2 Mar 2025. Describes an 'ABC Factorial' proof he says was sent to a number theory journal, desk-rejected, and is awaiting a referee. He writes: 'I decided to discuss it with the new Claude Sonnet 3.7 in case it found new errors.' He reports the model 'didn't [find errors] and suggested that I look at Brocard's equation', and says a modification of his method solves Brocard's equation (n! + 1 = m^2). The post gives no proof text. The subject is the namesake equation, not primes between consecutive prime squares.
events.revisions: None found.
events.delivers: Self-reported claim on the namesake equation n! + 1 = m^2. Does not bear on this statement.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Self-reported, unrefereed, and no proof text given. The AI system's contribution, as the author describes it, was to suggest the namesake equation as a next problem, not to supply anything on this statement.
events.direction: Not bearing on this statement (namesake).

events.what_happened: Abderrahim Makki Naciri, 2025 paper in Integers on the Brocard-Ramanujan equation n! + 1 = x^2. Per the erdosproblems.com thread for #398 (opened) and a search excerpt, for any integer k >= 2 the equation has only finitely many solutions if x +/- 1 is k-free or has fewer than k prime divisors; if x +/- 1 is 7-free then n = 4, 5, 7 are the only solutions. The Integers PDF returned unreadable binary, so these details are second-hand.
events.revisions: Not checked.
events.delivers: Finiteness results for the namesake equation under hypotheses. Not Brocard's conjecture.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (different question).
events.direction: Partial result on a namesake equation. Not bearing on this statement.

events.what_happened: A paper titled 'A short solution for Brocard-Ramanujans' problem (Erdos' conjecture) and its generalization' by Ahmad Sabihi, posted to the erdosproblems.com forum thread for #398 by user Alfaiz on 19 Oct 2025. The thread gives no date for the paper itself; one search excerpt says 2017. The paper's subject is the namesake equation n! + 1 = x^2, not primes between prime squares. Forum comments: Thomas Bloom wrote 'This paper has not been published in any peer-reviewed journal it seems', and that the methods look elementary, so a valid elementary proof seems unlikely. StijnC found a specific error: the claim that p^2 <= n! relates to divisibility is wrong, with a counterexample at n = 32, A = 17. StijnC also shared a ChatGPT opinion on the paper and said AI 'can check a long paper quickly than humans'. Commenter Dogmachine said failing 'GPT-level checking' would be 'pretty telling'.
events.revisions: None found. The date is the forum posting date, not the paper's own date.
events.delivers: Claimed: a short solution of the Brocard-Ramanujan equation (namesake). Nothing on primes between consecutive prime squares.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (namesake only).

checked_by.qualification: Forum participant; credentials not stated in the thread
checked_by.what_they_did: Identified a specific counterexample to a claimed step (n = 32, A = 17) and said the step is wrong
Noted no peer-reviewed publication and that the methods look elementary

events.doubts: The thread reports a specific error in a claimed step (counterexample at n = 32, A = 17), and says the author had not submitted the paper anywhere and had not corrected it. I did not check whether the author has responded since. The paper has no references.
events.direction: Toward proof of the namesake equation (claimed). The thread reports an error. Not bearing on this statement.

events.what_happened: J. M. Flagg, Louis H. Kauffman and Divyamaan Sahoo, 'Primes Between Squares -- Commentary on Appendix 8 of Laws Of Form', arXiv:2511.05603 (math.NT), submitted 6 Nov 2025, 61 pages. A commentary and guide to Spencer-Brown's Appendix 8, which claims at least two primes between any consecutive squared numbers. The abstract names only the Legendre question. It does not mention Brocard's conjecture.
events.revisions: v1 only (6 Nov 2025).
events.delivers: No new result. Describes the 1969 two-prime claim and says its proofs mix rigorous arguments with stated facts that 'would be considered conjectures by most number theorists'.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The commentary delivers no result.
events.doubts: It explains the appendix without judging completeness and does not name the conjectural lemmas. It does not address Brocard.
events.direction: Describes a two-prime claim without judging it.

events.what_happened: Marc Chamberland and Armin Straub, 'Weakening the Legendre Conjecture', arXiv:2602.22502 (26 Feb 2026). Reviews Legendre's conjecture and recent progress on primes between consecutive larger powers. Assuming RH, shows primes between x^(2+delta) and (x+1)^(2+delta) for delta >= 1/4, combining a result of Carneiro, Milinovich and Soundararajan with a Sorenson-Webster computation. The full text states that Legendre's conjecture remains open, that Oppermann's conjecture is verified only for n up to 7.05x10^13, and that no unconditional result of at least two primes between consecutive squares is stated. Does not mention Grah or Brocard's conjecture.
events.revisions: One version (v1, 26 Feb 2026).
events.delivers: Conditional (RH) result for powers, not consecutive squares. Neighbour, not Brocard.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Not bearing on this statement. Relevant as a later review that treats the Legendre statement as open and does not cite Grah.

events.what_happened: Peter J. Campbell, 'On the Existence of Integers with at Most 3 Prime Factors Between Every Pair of Consecutive Squares', arXiv:2603.10356. Improves the Dudek-Johnston bound from 4 to 3 prime factors, with computation for small n and a sieve argument with explicit constants for larger n. Brocard is not mentioned.

summary: I ran 36 web searches on the name, the alternative names (Brocard-Ramanujan, Brocard's problem / equation), the neighbouring conjectures (Legendre, Andrica, Oppermann, Cramér), AI-specific terms, and the places AI results are collected, and I opened about 30 sources. No accepted resolution, disproof or partial result has appeared since 26 January 2024. Three in-window items bear on the statement. (1) Grah (arXiv:2412.12311, posted 16 Dec 2024, revised Aug 2025) states an unconditional Theorem 6.8 (at least two primes between successive perfect squares) and a Proposition 6.11 (pi(p_{n+1}^2) - pi(p_n^2) >= 2d_n). Since d_n >= 2 for n >= 2, I infer that Proposition 6.11 gives Brocard's inequality for every n >= 2. The paper calls Proposition 6.11 a refinement of Brocard and does not draw that conclusion. The proof of Theorem 6.6, on which Theorem 6.8 depends, is not in the text I could read (the HTML copy is truncated and the PDF is unreadable). The paper also treats Legendre's conjecture as open and derives only a conditional one-prime result, while an unconditional two-prime theorem would imply Legendre's one-prime statement, so the two parts are in tension. No citing paper, referee report or expert response was found, and the 2026 Chamberland-Straub review does not cite it. (2) Vega (Preprints.org, Aug-Sep 2024) claims a proof of Oppermann's conjecture and says that proof also gives Brocard. It is labelled not peer-reviewed, its method changed between versions, and at least one reported version is conditional. I could not open the version texts (HTTP 403). (3) MathWorld and OEIS A050216 (Jan 2025) report a finite check to n <= 4x10^5. That is an instance count and does not settle a universal claim. Earlier claims: Mitra-Paul-Sarkar (2009) and Paz (2013) are conditional; Furones (2012) was withdrawn at v7; Sabihi (2016-2018) claims an Oppermann-route proof and is unrefereed; Visser (2018) claims an explicit check for all primes p < 2^32 through an implication chain, which conflicts in scale with MathWorld's 4x10^5 and whose method is not described; Feliksiak (2021) claims a proof I could not open (HTTP 403). The 1969 Spencer-Brown appendix claims the same two-prime statement as Grah's Theorem 6.8, and a 2025 commentary says its proofs rest partly on conjectural facts. Namesake noise: Brocard's problem (n! + 1 = m^2) has several 2024-2026 claims (Karimullah, Clements, Sabihi 2025, Naciri 2025), none about the prime-square statement. Close calls: whether Grah's Theorem 6.8 and its prerequisite Theorem 6.6 hold decides the in-window status, and I could not verify either. Visser's range and MathWorld's disagree, and Vega's excerpts conflict on which version says what. AI involvement: no source on this statement names an AI system. The Clements post names Claude Sonnet 3.7, but for the namesake equation, and the system's contribution there was a suggestion of direction. OpenAI's October 2026 manuscript repository (openai/math) has no Brocard or prime-gap entry: the README overview has none, and I read all six chunks of its CONTENTS.md (about 636k characters) without finding one. The DeepMind formal-conjectures GitHub search for 'Brocard' returned no files. The AlphaEvolve abstract does not mention it. Grah's acknowledgements and any AI statement were not reached, so the AI check on Grah is partial.
competing_reading: Read Grah's Proposition 6.11 as a real route to Brocard. The argument is short and elementary: the squares between p_n and p_{n+1} split the interval into d_n consecutive-square intervals, each holding at least two primes by Theorem 6.8, and d_n >= 2. On that reading the whole question reduces to Theorem 6.8 and its prerequisite Theorem 6.6, and a December 2024 preprint would count as a resolution if the judging pass accepts Theorem 6.8. The opposing reading: Theorem 6.8 would unconditionally settle a weak form of Legendre's conjecture, which the same paper treats as open and derives only conditionally, which a 2025 commentary says is supported only partly by standard arguments, and which no later review cites. A result of that size would normally draw attention, and none has appeared in 22 months. On this reading Grah is an unrefereed claim that has not been engaged with, and the in-window status is 'no accepted progress'. Vega's and Visser's claims are weaker still: Vega rests on an unrefereed Oppermann proof, and Visser's computation is undescribed and disagrees in scale with MathWorld.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A readable full text of Grah (arXiv:2412.12311), specifically the statement and proof of Theorem 6.6 and the proof of Theorem 6.8, and whether either uses Section 6.1's Legendre-conjecture bound or Conjecture 1.1; a Lean formalisation of Theorem 6.8 and Proposition 6.11 would settle the mathematics. (b) An expert referee report or public verification of Theorem 6.8, which would also settle the Legendre one-prime statement, or a retraction or a published error. (c) A citing paper that uses or rejects Grah, in either direction. (d) For Vega: the full texts of Preprints.org v1 to v4, to see whether the Brocard claim is unconditional in any version. (e) For Feliksiak: the ScienceOpen text, to fix the date and read the argument. (f) For Visser: the computation method for p < 2^32, and an explanation of the difference from MathWorld's n <= 4x10^5. (g) For Spencer-Brown: the appendix's proofs and any refereeing, which would settle the 1969 two-prime claim independently of Grah.

events.credibility_reason: The two-prime claim would imply Brocard only through a counting step that the source does not make. The 2025 commentary says the proofs rest partly on facts most number theorists would call conjectures, and a 2026 review states that no unconditional two-prime result is known.

events.credibility_reason: The unconditional Theorem 6.8 would settle a strong form of Legendre's conjecture, yet the same paper calls Legendre open and derives the weaker one-prime statement only conditionally. The prerequisite Theorem 6.6 has no proof that could be found, and Section 6.1 invokes Legendre's conjecture. There has been no uptake in 22 months on a landmark claim, and the 2026 Chamberland-Straub review states that no unconditional two-prime result exists. The paper never draws the Brocard conclusion; it comes from the researcher's inference.

judgement.why: The only events after the snapshot that claim the whole statement are Vega's Oppermann note and Grah's preprint. Both are set aside as not credible, because several F10 signals are present at once, not merely because nobody has reviewed them. Grah was the closest call. The step from Proposition 6.11 to Brocard (d_n >= 2, so at least four primes) is sound if Theorem 6.8 holds. But Theorem 6.8 contradicts the paper's own treatment of Legendre's conjecture as open, its prerequisite Theorem 6.6 is unproved in the text available, nobody has engaged with it in 22 months on a landmark, and a 2026 review states that no such result is known. Taken together, these signals outweigh treating it as merely doubtful. The MathWorld/OEIS check and Visser's check are finite instances. The Brocard-Ramanujan items, the Legendre, Andrica and almost-prime results, and Tyszka are variants. Clements names Claude Sonnet 3.7, but systems[] is empty and the model only suggested a namesake problem, so ai_role is none. Before the snapshot, every claim of the whole statement is unreviewed, withdrawn or not credible, so none of them tiers as resolved.
judgement.doubts: Grah's Theorem 6.6 and its acknowledgements were not read (the HTML copy was truncated), so both the credibility call and the AI check on Grah rest on partial text. Grah's paper does not itself draw the >= 4 conclusion. For Spencer-Brown, the scope of 'whole' depends on the same counting inference. Naciri's date is year-only (2025), but it lies after the snapshot regardless; it was set to null only to follow the year-only rule, and it is a variant either way.
